opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that science, at its core, is a kind of inverse problem. You observe the world, you see data, and you're trying to infer the underlying causal mechanisms that generated that data. What's unusual about science compared to a lot of machine learning is that the thing you're trying to recover is a *model*, a structured, causal, generative explanation, not just a predictor.

Autumn was our attempt to take that seriously in a setting small enough to actually make progress on. We take these simple grid-world video games, and the agent or the system watches someone play, sees the frames, sees the actions, and the task is to recover the program that generated the game: the objects, their dynamics, the rules for how they interact, what happens when you click or press a key. So it's literally inferring source code from observations.

Why does that count as science, and not just some program synthesis exercise? A few reasons. First, the hypothesis space is programs, which is really what scientific theories are: compositional, causal descriptions that let you predict what would happen under interventions you've never seen. Second, a lot of the hard part is the same as in real science. There are latent variables. Things happen that aren't directly caused by anything you can see, so you have to posit hidden state. A lot of our technical work was about how to invent those latent variables, the analogue of a scientist saying "there must be some unobserved quantity, call it a field or a particle, that explains this regularity."

Third, and this is where I think it gets really interesting, it's not passive. Real science involves experimentation. If you just watch a recording you'll often have ambiguity, and the right move is to go into the game and poke at it, do the thing that discriminates between your hypotheses. So we've been thinking a lot about active experimental design inside these environments: how do you choose actions that are most informative about the underlying program?

So I see it as a microcosm. It's obviously much simpler than inferring the laws of biology or physics, but it has the essential structure: observation, hypothesis formation in a rich compositional language, latent causes, and intervention. If we can't build systems that do this well in a world we fully control and where we know the ground truth, it's hard to believe we'll build systems that do it for the real world. And conversely, getting it right here teaches us a lot about what an automated scientist actually needs.

r001.rationale: The response describes recovering the game’s causal program—its objects, dynamics, and interaction rules—from observations as understanding the mechanisms that generate the world.

r002.rationale: It presents programs as structured causal descriptions of the game’s dynamics and says the program includes objects, their dynamics, and rules, supporting the idea that the evolving world is described by a program.

r003.rationale: The response mentions inferring a program from play traces and separately discusses latent variables, but does not identify joint inference of hidden state and program from interaction traces as Autumn’s research question.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that science, at its core, is the construction of models of the world from observation, and that's exactly what we're asking the system to do in Autumn. The difference is that we've shrunk the world down to something tractable.

So in Autumn, you're given a grid world, a little two-dimensional environment, and you observe it unfolding over time. Things move around, things appear, things collide, you take actions and the world responds. And the task is to recover the program, the actual causal structure, that generated what you're seeing. You don't get the rules. You just get the frames, and you have to work backwards to the generative process.

And when you frame it that way, it maps really cleanly onto what a scientist does. A physicist is looking at observations of the world and trying to infer the underlying laws. They're not just predicting the next frame, they're trying to find the compact, mechanistic explanation that accounts for everything they've seen, and ideally generalizes to things they haven't seen. That's the key distinction I'd draw with a lot of contemporary machine learning. A video prediction model can get very good at predicting pixels without ever recovering anything like the actual mechanism. In Autumn, we care about recovering the mechanism itself, the source code, because that's what gives you explanation, that's what gives you compositional generalization, and that's what lets you intervene and reason counterfactually.

There are also a few things that make the game-inference setting feel genuinely scientific rather than just a pattern-matching exercise. One is that there's hidden state. A lot of these worlds have latent variables you can't directly observe, like an internal counter or a mode the game is in, and you have to posit those as part of your theory. That's a very scientific move, right, postulating unobservable entities to explain observed regularities. Another is that it's active. You're not just a passive observer, you can act in the world and run what are effectively experiments to disambiguate between competing hypotheses. And a third is that there's a strong inductive bias toward simplicity. Among all the programs consistent with the data, you want the one that's most parsimonious, which is basically Occam's razor operationalized.

So I'd say we're not using "science" as a loose metaphor. We're trying to build a minimal, controlled instance of the actual scientific process, where we know the ground truth, so we can study what it would take for a machine to do theory formation at all. And then the hope is that the mechanisms that work there, the program synthesis, the handling of latent causes, the active experimentation, those scale toward domains where we don't know the ground truth, which is of course where it would actually matter.

r001.rationale: It describes recovering the program and causal mechanism that generated observed dynamics as finding an explanation of how the world works.

r002.rationale: It presents the program as the world’s generative mechanism and says hidden variables are part of the theory used to explain its observed behavior.

r003.rationale: It mentions inferring latent variables and using actions as experiments, but does not identify joint inference of hidden state and program from interaction traces as the research question.

astra-6.text:
I think it captures a very basic idea of science: you observe what a system does, and you try to construct a model that explains how those observations are generated. In this case, the observations are the frames of a video game, and the model is a program. It might say that an object moves according to a particular rule, or that when two objects collide, something happens.

What's interesting is that you’re trying to recover an executable explanation. You can run the program and ask whether it reproduces what you saw. You can also ask what it predicts in a situation you haven’t observed—what would happen if you pressed a different button, for example—and then test that prediction against the game.

There’s an important qualification, though: you generally can’t infer the unique original source code from its behavior. Many programs could produce the same observations. So the scientific task is to find an explanation that fits the evidence and generalizes, and then identify experiments that distinguish it from competing explanations. The game gives you a very concrete setting in which to study that process.

r001.rationale: The response describes constructing an executable model that explains observed game behavior, framing this as a scientific way to understand the system.

r002.rationale: It says a program can model the game's behavior, but does not propose that a world's evolving hidden state is best described by a program.

r003.rationale: It discusses inferring a program from video frames and testing predictions, but does not identify joint inference of hidden state and program from interaction traces as Autumn's research question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a very concrete instance of the scientific process. You have a system that you can observe—in this case, a video game—but you don’t have access to the mechanism that generated those observations. So you propose a model, expressed as a program, run it, and compare its behavior with what you actually see. When it disagrees, you revise the program.

What makes a game interesting is that you can intervene. You can press a button, move a character, or push one object into another, and ask whether your proposed rules predict what happens. That’s analogous to doing an experiment to distinguish between competing scientific hypotheses.

The aim doesn’t have to be recovering the exact text of the original source code. Different programs could explain the same observations. The interesting question is whether you recover an underlying set of rules that explains what you’ve seen and predicts what will happen in situations you haven’t seen. In that sense, the inferred program is a scientific theory of the game.

r001.rationale: It describes inferring a program of game rules that explains observations and predicts what happens, calling that program a scientific theory of the game.

r002.rationale: It presents a program as a model of the game’s rules, but does not say that the world’s evolving hidden state is best described by a program.

r003.rationale: It mentions interventions and comparing predictions with observations, but does not identify joint inference of hidden state and the underlying program from interaction traces as Autumn’s research question.
